content: The ShengTing platform is used to generate sequencing libraries, which are then processed on either the MinION or GridION platforms developed by Oxford Nanopore Technologies. These platforms are employed for sequencing data processing and are integrated with a secure online application, the TBseq® Web App, which includes databases for interpreting results. Two health-related questions were formulated using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) framework to guide evidence search, retrieval, and analysis. The first question addressed whether targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) should be used as the initial test to diagnose drug resistance in individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis (TB). This question specifically examined resistance to rifampicin, isoniazid, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, using phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) and whole genome sequencing (WGS) as reference standards. The second question focused on whether targeted NGS should be used to diagnose drug resistance in individuals with bacteriologically confirmed rifampicin-resistant pulmonary TB, evaluating resistance to drugs such as isoniazid, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, pyrazinamide, bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, amikacin, ethambutol, and streptomycin. A comprehensive search of three databases (Medline, Ovid Embase, and Scopus) was conducted to identify relevant studies, with no date restrictions. The initial search was performed on September 7, 2022, and repeated on January 17, 2023. Additionally, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued a public call for data and contacted experts in the field to identify unpublished data. No data were found regarding the impact of targeted NGS on patient-level health outcomes, such as time to treatment or treatment success. For diagnostic accuracy analysis, all available data from the literature were included after correspondence with authors. An individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis was conducted instead of a classical meta-analysis due to the small size of most studies, particularly for newer and repurposed drugs. This approach allowed for the inclusion of relevant covariates in the model and controlled for repeated testing on the same samples using different platforms. Multivariable models included fixed effects such as rifampicin resistance determined by Xpert MTB/RIF® or Xpert Ultra®, semi-quantitative cycle threshold (CT) values, and duplicate sample representation. For models assessing diagnostic accuracy in people living with HIV (PLHIV), HIV test results were included as a covariate. Study site was treated as a random effect. The models were run in Stata (version 17) using the melogit command, and outputs were transformed using the margins command. The certainty of evidence for pooled studies was systematically assessed for each PICO question using the GRADE approach, which evaluates evidence quality based on factors such as risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, and other considerations. Evidence quality was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low, depending on the severity of identified issues. For PICO 1, the pooled sensitivity of targeted NGS was at least 95% for isoniazid, moxifloxacin, and ethambutol, over 93% for rifampicin and levofloxacin, and 88% for pyrazinamide. The pooled specificity was at least 96% for all drugs. Indeterminate test results ranged from 9% (levofloxacin and moxifloxacin) to 18% (pyrazinamide), with higher rates observed in samples with lower bacterial loads. The reference standard was culture-based phenotypic DST for isoniazid, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin, and a combination of phenotypic DST and WGS for rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. For PICO 2, the pooled sensitivity among individuals with rifampicin-resistant TB was ≥95% for isoniazid, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ethambutol, and streptomycin, and 90% for pyrazinamide. Sensitivity was lower for bedaquiline (68%), linezolid (69%), clofazimine (70%), and amikacin (87%). The pooled specificity was ≥95% for all drugs except streptomycin (75%). Indeterminate test results ranged from 9% (levofloxacin and moxifloxacin) to 21% (ethambutol). The reference standard was culture-based phenotypic DST for most drugs, with a combination of phenotypic DST and WGS for ethambutol and pyrazinamide. The cost and cost-effectiveness of targeted NGS were assessed through a systematic review of the literature and a generalized model-based cost-effectiveness analysis commissioned by WHO. Costing data were adjusted to 2021 US dollars, and findings were synthesized descriptively due to heterogeneity in study methodologies and outcomes.
